purpose: Shared input for Phase 1 (corroboration) and Phase 2 (triage). Derived mechanically; anchors below are for reconciliation, not for adoption.

fragile_conclusions.title: Notify a traveller the moment they qualify for a right they already hold — not only when something has gone wrong.
fragile_conclusions.body: Trainline offers to notify a traveller when they QUALIFY FOR DELAY COMPENSATION, not merely when a delay occurs. It needs only the itinerary and the compensation rules — no inventory, no balance sheet, no insurance licence. Luma's scenario already assumes it holds the itinerary.
fragile_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture, in rail. No air, hotel or activity equivalent was observed anywhere in the roster — this is a single-competitor, single-vertical proof, not a corroborated pattern.

fragile_conclusions.title: Show what each ranking choice costs, on the control itself.
fragile_conclusions.body: Kayak's sort tabs display the trade-off of each option directly — e.g. 35 € / 7h 14m against 47 € / 1h 25m — so the cost of a choice is visible before it is made. This is not a new axis; it is making an existing trade-off legible at the point of choice.
fragile_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture, single competitor. No other product observed shows the consequence of a sort choice on the control itself.

fragile_conclusions.title: Compare accommodation by one total price, never a nightly rate, at the moment of comparison.
fragile_conclusions.body: Airbnb shows total price only at search-results time (e.g. '203 € en total') and never a per-night figure; every other accommodation competitor observed leads with a nightly rate that must be multiplied and has fees added later. This removes arithmetic a first-time traveller cannot yet reliably do. (Airbnb itself relaxes this at checkout, once the traveller has already chosen — the nightly rate reappears there.)
fragile_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture. Airbnb is the only competitor doing this; every other observed competitor does the opposite, which is corroborating context, not independent confirmation that total-only is better.

fragile_conclusions.title: Compute an ease/effort ranking axis for accommodation and on-site transport specifically — not for flights, where it is already solved, or activities, where duration is not yet a structured field anywhere observed.
fragile_conclusions.body: The corrected finding from this round: effort is ranked where it is already measured (flights, rail) and ignored where it is not (accommodation). Trainline is the existence proof for HOW to phrase it — effort first, price as the tiebreaker, explained in one sentence.
fragile_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on a capture that explicitly narrows its own scope: the zero-effort-axis accommodation finding is measured on 3 products; the flights comparison rests on 1 product (Google). Both scope limits are stated in the source capture itself, not added here.

fragile_conclusions.title: A button that looks live can silently do nothing.
fragile_conclusions.body: Booking.com's primary ‘I'll reserve’ control produced no navigation until a room quantity was selected — and nothing on the page states this. It was never disabled; it was enabled and did nothing.

fragile_conclusions.title: Being signed out doesn't stop a sign-in prompt from interrupting your search.
fragile_conclusions.body: Navigating a signed-out Booking.com session to search results opened a Google One Tap sign-in prompt as a second tab.

fragile_conclusions.title: Look at things to do near where you're staying, and the trip you were just building disappears — dates and all.
fragile_conclusions.body: Moving from Airbnb's accommodation search to Experiences drops the dates entirely, even though both sit under the same account.

fragile_conclusions.title: Three products, one afternoon, three different guesses at where you are — and none of them asked.
fragile_conclusions.body: Google's AI planner: ‘Estás en Toronto’. Kayak: origin pre-filled ‘Madrid (MAD)’. Skyscanner: ‘Salida desde: Marsella (MRS)’. Each states its guess as fact.

fragile_conclusions.title: Saying no to an add-on is written back to you as a confession.
fragile_conclusions.body: Expedia's insurance decline reads: ‘I'm willing to risk my $358.59 stay in Lisbon.’ A traveller who simply doesn't want the product is made to state a risk they are taking.

all_conclusions.title: Nobody does both halves.
sources: WORLD.md § 2 The finding that should govern the rest

all_conclusions.title: Protection is sold as a product, or included as a property of the booking — and the seam between the two is covered by neither.
The disruption chain degrades at every hop, and no single participant is lying or failing on its own.
Effort is ranked exactly where it is already measured, and computed nowhere else.
Control over ranking and explanation of ranking look like a trade-off — until one product has both.
Conversational AI is observed as baseline, not as a differentiator — on the products this round actually reached.
A confident wrong answer beats an honest question, almost everywhere.
Notify a traveller the moment they qualify for a right they already hold — not only when something has gone wrong.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture, in rail. No air, hotel or activity equivalent was observed anywhere in the roster — this is a single-competitor, single-vertical proof, not a corroborated pattern.

all_conclusions.title: Show what each ranking choice costs, on the control itself.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture, single competitor. No other product observed shows the consequence of a sort choice on the control itself.

all_conclusions.title: Compare accommodation by one total price, never a nightly rate, at the moment of comparison.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on one Verified capture. Airbnb is the only competitor doing this; every other observed competitor does the opposite, which is corroborating context, not independent confirmation that total-only is better.

all_conclusions.title: Publish what a protection or guarantee does NOT cover, in the same document that sells it — and go further than any observed competitor by surfacing it at the moment of comparison or payment, not only in a help centre.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on two Verified captures of the SAME competitor. The plain-language-boundary half of this recommendation has a positive example (Airbnb). The surface-it-at-the-decision half has no positive example anywhere in the round — it is a gap the evidence identifies, not a pattern the evidence confirms works.

all_conclusions.title: When a traveller can decline an add-on, ask neutrally — never phrase the decline as a confession.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on a direct, paired comparison — both captures Verified, same funnel position, comparable amounts. The strongest-evidenced recommendation in this set.

all_conclusions.title: Compute an ease/effort ranking axis for accommodation and on-site transport specifically — not for flights, where it is already solved, or activities, where duration is not yet a structured field anywhere observed.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on a capture that explicitly narrows its own scope: the zero-effort-axis accommodation finding is measured on 3 products; the flights comparison rests on 1 product (Google). Both scope limits are stated in the source capture itself, not added here.

all_conclusions.title: Model the trip as one object across booking types before designing individual screens for each one — a data-model decision, not a UX one.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on three findings of mixed confidence: F78 and F101 are plain Verified; F68 (the seam) is Verified as description of stated scopes, with its consequence for a real traveller marked Inferred. This recommendation inherits the weaker of the three.

all_conclusions.title: Design the retention mechanism explicitly for someone on their first trip — nothing on the roster currently does.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on four Verified findings, each scope-limited to 'absence on this page only, not the whole product' — stated in the source captures, carried through here rather than smoothed away.

all_conclusions.title: Decide, before any screen is designed, whether disruption protection is something Luma sells or something Luma is.
all_conclusions.rests_on: Rests on the Hopper capture's own framing (Verified) plus the disruption-chain synthesis (Insight 3, itself carrying a compound confidence). This is a business-model decision the evidence poses; it does not answer it.

all_conclusions.title: You can't tell whether a recommendation is impartial or paid for.
A button that looks live can silently do nothing.
Being signed out doesn't stop a sign-in prompt from interrupting your search.
Real protection can exist and still be invisible exactly when you'd want it.
The moment you most need help is the one you're least likely to find a route to.
If this is your first trip, no loyalty programme on the roster has anything to say to you.
Look at things to do near where you're staying, and the trip you were just building disappears — dates and all.
Three products, one afternoon, three different guesses at where you are — and none of them asked.
A cookie banner with no single-click way to say no, before you've searched anything.
Saying no to an add-on is written back to you as a confession.

uncited_findings.claim: Accessibility is a contractual term, not only a design commitment — section A11 'Accessibility requests' sits in the Terms of Service.
The statement names no accessibility standard and makes no conformance claim.
Accessibility of the actual travel experience is routed away from Booking.com to the supplier.
Across three first-party documents Booking.com consistently occupies an intermediary position and pushes responsibility outward at every layer.
Booking.com DOES disclose that commercial terms affect ranking — so a blanket claim that competitors never explain their recommendations does not hold here.
Loyalty membership changes the ranking surface by exactly one axis, and that axis is another PRICE axis.
No account is required to reach the booking form. There is no sign-in wall and no guest-checkout prompt either — the question is simply never asked.
Booking.com's answer to multi-type trip attachment is three opt-in checkboxes inside the booking form.
Expedia carries six verticals to Booking.com's four booking types, adding Packages and Cruises — but presents a far smaller link surface on the homepage.
For an identical city and date range, Expedia returns 499 properties where Booking.com returns 4,194 — roughly an eightfold difference.
Expedia offers no ranking axis based on effort, ease, stress or confidence. Enumerated positively from the opened control.
Expedia collapses guest details and payment onto ONE page; Booking.com splits them across two, with no payment field present on its details step.
Google Travel exposes four decision-support surfaces that neither Booking.com nor Expedia offers anywhere in their accommodation journey.
Google Travel hands off rather than sells. No 'Book on Google' surface was present on the accommodation result.
Google Travel offers three ranking axes: an opaque default, price, and a quality proxy. None concerns effort, ease, stress or confidence.
Google Travel is the only product observed that tells a traveller what a normal price looks like before they search.
Authentication unlocks exactly one capability on Google Travel, and it is a functional one — persistent price monitoring — not a discount.
Two products, two matched-pair diffs, one extra capability each — but of opposite kinds.
Google Flights publishes an explicit all-in pricing commitment — the stated opposite of drip pricing.
Google Flights explicitly addresses a traveller who has not decided, in its own copy.
On a live route, Google states whether the current price is normal and when to buy — without requiring a booking, an account, or a commitment.
Google Flights surfaces a comparison dimension that is neither price, quality proxy, nor distance: carbon emissions, expressed relative to the route average.
Emissions is a selectable sort axis, not merely a displayed attribute. F-34's OWED test is settled.
Kayak ships a standalone Flight Tracker at /tracker — a direct analogue of a named Luma core feature.
The ad-landing variant renders the same product surface as the clean URL. The tracking parameters produced no observable difference.
Kayak's AI planner ships a designed empty state. This is the first empty state observed anywhere in the round across four competitors.
Kayak's travel AI accepts photo and file upload as planning input, not just text.
The planner asserts the traveller's location unprompted, and asserted it incorrectly.
Kayak labels paid placements explicitly and in the first person of the advertiser.
From a flight result set, Kayak asks whether the traveller wants bus prices.
Two meta-search products state opposite pricing commitments for the same product category.
Kayak sells combined itineraries assembled from separate airlines, each governed by its own conditions, with no single carrier owning the journey.
Kayak's handoff on this result went directly to the airline that operates the flight, not to a reseller.
Within a single Kayak result set, the protection a traveller ends up with varies enormously — and nothing in the ranking, sorting or price display reflects that.
Crossing the handoff, the traveller loses all trace of the product that sent them and immediately faces a fresh consent gate.
The meta-search handoff deposits the traveller, pre-selected, into the airline's most restrictive fare family.
Iberia states an all-in total with a named exception. Kayak, which sent the traveller here, states that its prices exclude baggage fees.
Iberia's airport services are bundled with Business class, not sold as add-ons. The page title scopes them to a fare class in its own words.
Business goal 5 assumes airport services are a purchasable product. On the first supplier examined they are a fare-class entitlement, which changes who Luma would be selling to.
Iberia ships a chat assistant, 'Ibot', present on this page.
Iberia Club is the only loyalty programme of the three examined whose currency can be earned without travelling at all.
Iberia Club extends programme benefits to children as a stated feature.
Skyscanner offers search with no destination at all — 'Explora cualquier lugar'.
Skyscanner's own FAQ headings directly address the confusion the handoff creates.
Hopper ships a family of flexibility products, not a single one.
Hopper's web surface permits search but gates its differentiating products behind the app.
Airbnb offers three payment timings, one of which defers the entire cost at no additional charge.
Airbnb states whether the price is normal, at the moment of payment.
Airbnb states that its algorithm deliberately favours variety — showing different hosts, characteristics and price points rather than the single best-scoring set.
The five stated factors contain no commission, advertising or paid-placement term.
Airbnb shows accommodation as a total for the stay and experiences as a price per traveller. The same product uses two conventions in two verticals.
'Descubrir' (Discover) is a top-level navigation item, alongside 'Opinión' (Review).
Tripadvisor's primary verticals are things to do, hotels and restaurants. No flights vertical was present on the homepage.
Tripadvisor states the basis of its rankings on the results surface.
Rentalcars.com states on its own homepage that it is part of Booking Holdings — the same parent as Booking.com, competitor 1.
Rentalcars makes an explicit no-hidden-charges claim on the homepage.
The cancellation promise carries a qualifier that most travellers will not weigh.
Booking.com, Kayak and Rentalcars.com — competitors 1, 4 and 9 on the roster — are all Booking Holdings companies. Verified from first-party statements on two of the three.
Trainline's search form carries a PRE-CHECKED Booking.com Genius cross-sell which, on search, opened a Booking.com hotel search in the original tab — with dates that are not the travel dates.
Trainline surfaces duration and change-count per result and offers a 'Direct only' filter.
Omio's consent modal states it shares personal data with 164 partners.
Omio accepts city, station, airport OR port in a single origin field and compares across four transport modes in one result set.
Rome2Rio presents duration and price together, per transport mode, in one view — including modes no other roster competitor surfaces.
Citymapper presents transit options with frequency, calories and cross-mode alternatives alongside price and duration — three attributes absent from every other competitor in the roster.
Across the roster, effort is now observed measured in three different units, and which unit is used depends entirely on what the vertical can compute.
TripIt sells pre-trip entry-requirement guidance as a named Pro feature.
Qatar Airways sells the loyalty currency, the STATUS points, and a paid subscription to the loyalty programme itself.
Qatar Airways treats the airport as a destination with its own product line, unlike Iberia where airport services are a Business-class entitlement.

F-108 inferred that lounge access is indirectly purchasable, because lounge access sits at Silver and Qpoints are sold — but flagged that many programmes exclude PURCHASED points from tier qualification, and that the inference was unverified.
Privilege Club runs three distinct currencies.
Qatar Airways publishes a unit price for loyalty status: USD 25 per Qpoint.
aa.com redirects to americanairlines.es for a Spanish-locale session, serving a materially thinner site — 43 links against a US site that hosts a full Customer Service Plan.
